This page is the interactive version of the lesson notes (PDF). Each section
starts with a problem in a game. Then it explains the idea behind it. It ends
with a **Do it** task and one set of questions. Every question on this page
has its answer: try first, then check.

## Key terms

{{< glossary homogeneous-coordinates translation-matrix transformation-matrix composite-transformation trs-matrix 3d scaling rotation-axis rotation-matrix forward-vector >}}

## 10.1 Why a 2 × 2 matrix cannot move a shape

- Every 2 × 2 matrix sends (0, 0) to (0, 0): it can scale and turn, but
  never move.
- **Homogeneous coordinates:** the point (x, y) becomes **(x, y, 1)**.
- Transformations then become 3 × 3 matrices; their last row is always
  (0, 0, 1).
- To read the point again, drop the last 1: (7, 3, 1) is (7, 3).

![A 3 × 3 matrix can move the origin.](images/homogeneous.png){width=92%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
A point needs w = 1, not 0. With w = 0 the move is lost.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Add the third coordinate"}
Write (4, −2), (0, 3) and (0, 0) in homogeneous coordinates. Then multiply
any 2 × 2 matrix by (0, 0). What do you always get?

::: {.check}
(4, −2, 1), (0, 3, 1), (0, 0, 1). Any 2 × 2 matrix × (0, 0) = (0, 0): it
cannot move the origin.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Three coordinates"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(2, 1, 0)|(1, 2, 1)"}
How do you write the point (2, 1) in homogeneous coordinates?
:   (2, 1, 1)

    Why: a point gets w = 1.

Which 2D point is (7, 3, 1)?
:   (7, 3)

    Why: drop the last 1.

What does any 2 × 2 matrix do to (0, 0)?
:   it keeps it at (0, 0)

    Why: every row times (0, 0) gives 0.

What is the last row of a 3 × 3 transformation matrix?
:   (0, 0, 1)

    Why: it keeps w = 1.
:::
:::

## 10.2 The translation matrix

- **T(tx, ty) = rows (1, 0, tx), (0, 1, ty), (0, 0, 1)**: the move is in the
  last column.
- T(5, 2) × (2, 1, 1) = (7, 3, 1): the same as (2, 1) + (5, 2).
- Undo it with T(−tx, −ty).

![The translation matrix T(tx, ty).](images/translate-matrix.png){width=92%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
tx and ty go into the last column, not the last row.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build T(−3, 4)"}
Write T(−3, 4) and multiply it by (5, 1, 1). Check with an addition.

::: {.check}
T(−3, 4) = rows (1, 0, −3), (0, 1, 4), (0, 0, 1); × (5, 1, 1) = (2, 5, 1). Check:
(5 − 3, 1 + 4).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · The translation matrix"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(4, −1, 1)|T(1, 4)"}
What is T(4, −1) × (2, 5, 1)?
:   (6, 4, 1)

    Why: (2 + 4, 5 − 1, 1).

Which matrix undoes T(4, −1)?
:   T(−4, 1)

    Why: move back by the opposite vector.

Where is the move in T(tx, ty)?
:   in the last column

    Why: the 1 of the point picks up the last column.

What is T(−3, 4) × (5, 1, 1)?
:   (2, 5, 1)

    Why: (5 − 3, 1 + 4, 1).
:::
:::

## 10.3 Scale, turn and move in one matrix

- Scale and turn become 3 × 3 too: the 2 × 2 matrix in the top-left corner;
  the last column and row are (0, 0, 1). S(2) = rows (2, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0),
  (0, 0, 1); R(90°) = rows (0, −1, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1).
- The **TRS matrix** M = T × R × S: first scale, then rotate, then translate
  (read from right to left).
- S(2), R(90°), T(5, 1): **M = rows (0, −2, 5), (2, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1)**.
- M × (1, 0, 1) = (5, 3). Step by step: (2, 0), (0, 2), (5, 3).
- The order matters: for (1, 0), T(2, 0) × R(90°) gives (2, 1), but
  R(90°) × T(2, 0) gives (0, 3).

![Scaling and rotation in 3 × 3.](images/scale-rotate-3x3.png){width=86%}

![M = T × R × S.](images/trs-chain.png){width=86%}

{{< sim file="sims/matrix-chain.html" poster="sims/matrix-chain.png" title="Matrix Chain: M = T × R × S" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
In M = T × R × S, S acts first, although it is written last. And the
bottom-right corner is always 1, never 0.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build M in Matrix Chain"}
Set scale 2, θ = 90°, tx = 5, ty = 1 and compare M with the bullet above.
Then set θ = 180°. Where does the nose (2, 0.3) go?

::: {.check}
θ = 90°: rows (0, −2, 5), (2, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1). θ = 180°: rows (−2, 0, 5),
(0, −2, 1), (0, 0, 1); the nose goes to (−4 + 5, −0.6 + 1) = (1, 0.4).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Scale, turn and TRS"}
M = T(5, 1) × R(90°) × S(2) = rows (0, −2, 5), (2, 0, 1), (0, 0, 1). Choose
the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(2, 5)|T first|(3, 2, 3)"}
What is S(3, 1) × (1, 2, 1)?
:   (3, 2, 1)

    Why: (3 × 1, 1 × 2, 1).

What is R(90°) × (2, 1, 1)?
:   (−1, 2, 1)

    Why: (−y, x) = (−1, 2); w stays 1.

Where does M send the point (1, 0)?
:   (5, 3)

    Why: (0 − 0 + 5, 2 + 0 + 1).

Where does M send the point (0, 1)?
:   (3, 1)

    Why: (0 − 2 + 5, 0 + 0 + 1).

Which matrix acts first in T × R × S?
:   S

    Why: read from right to left: S is next to the point.

What does R(90°) × T(2, 0) do to (1, 0)?
:   (0, 3)

    Why: move first: (3, 0); then turn: (0, 3).
:::
:::

## 10.4 Move and scale in 3D: 4 × 4 matrices

- A 3D point becomes **(x, y, z, 1)**; a direction (the way a cannon fires)
  is (x, y, z, 0): it is not moved.
- **T(tx, ty, tz)**: the 4 × 4 identity with (tx, ty, tz) in the last
  column. The crate (1, 0, 2) with T(3, 0, 4): (4, 0, 6).
- **S(sx, sy, sz)**: sx, sy, sz on the main diagonal, then 1.
  S(2, 3, 1) × (1, 1, 1) = (2, 3, 1).
- A uniform scale of 2 doubles each side, so the volume is 8 times bigger.

![The 4 × 4 translation matrix.](images/translate-4x4.png){width=86%}

![Scaling in 3D.](images/scale-3d.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
A 4 × 4 matrix needs four coordinates: w = 1 for a point, w = 0 for a
direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A pillar"}
Which scaling turns the unit cube into a pillar 1 wide, 4 tall and 1 deep?
Where does the corner (1, 1, 1) go? Then apply T(1, 2, 3) to the point
(4, 0, 0, 1) and to the direction (4, 0, 0, 0).

::: {.check}
S(1, 4, 1): (1, 1, 1) → (1, 4, 1). The point → (5, 2, 3, 1); the direction
stays (4, 0, 0, 0).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Move and scale in 3D"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(4, 0, 0, 1)|2 times|(3, 1, 6)"}
What is T(1, 2, 3) × (4, 0, 0, 1)?
:   (5, 2, 3, 1)

    Why: a point (w = 1) is moved: (4 + 1, 0 + 2, 0 + 3).

What is T(1, 2, 3) × (4, 0, 0, 0)?
:   (4, 0, 0, 0)

    Why: a direction (w = 0) is not moved.

Which matrix undoes T(1, 2, 3)?
:   T(−1, −2, −3)

    Why: move back by (−1, −2, −3).

What is S(2, 2, 2) × (1, −1, 3)?
:   (2, −2, 6)

    Why: every coordinate × 2.

A cube gets a uniform scale of 2. How much bigger is its volume?
:   8 times

    Why: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
:::
:::

## 10.5 Yaw: turning around the y-axis

- **R_y(θ) = rows (cos θ, 0, sin θ), (0, 1, 0), (−sin θ, 0, cos θ)**. y
  stays.
- Forward (0, 0, 1) goes to **(sin θ, 0, cos θ)**. A positive yaw turns to
  the right (seen from above).
- 90°: forward → (1, 0, 0). The right side (2, 0, 0) → (0, 0, −2).

![The yaw seen from above.](images/yaw.png){width=92%}

{{< sim file="sims/yaw-lab.html" poster="sims/yaw-lab.png" title="Yaw Lab: turning around the y-axis in 3D" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
Around y, the minus sign is in row 3. Check: R_y(90°) sends (0, 0, 1) to
(1, 0, 0).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Yaw by hand, check in Yaw Lab"}
Compute R_y(180°) × (0, 0, 1) and R_y(−90°) × (0, 0, 1). Then set the same
angles in **Yaw Lab** and compare.

::: {.check}
R_y(180°) × (0, 0, 1) = (0, 0, −1): backwards. R_y(−90°) × (0, 0, 1) =
(−1, 0, 0): to the left. Yaw Lab shows the same.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Yaw"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(0, 1, 0)|(1, 0, 1)"}
What is R_y(90°) × (0, 0, 1)?
:   (1, 0, 0)

    Why: (sin 90°, 0, cos 90°) = (1, 0, 0).

What is R_y(180°) × (3, 2, 1)?
:   (−3, 2, −1)

    Why: cos 180° = −1, sin 180° = 0: x and z change sign; y stays.

What is R_y(90°) × (2, 0, 0)?
:   (0, 0, −2)

    Why: row 1: 0; row 3: −1 × 2 = −2.

A player has a yaw of 30°. What is the forward vector?
:   (0.5, 0, 0.87)

    Why: (sin 30°, 0, cos 30°).

What is R_y(−90°) × (0, 0, 1)?
:   (−1, 0, 0)

    Why: (sin(−90°), 0, cos(−90°)) = (−1, 0, 0).
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Lighthouse {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

**Lighthouse** is a night game. The lighthouse stands at the origin. At the
yaw θ the beam points along **(sin θ, 0, cos θ)**. Ships wait 10 units away:
at (10, 0, 0), at (0, 0, −10), at (5, 0, 8.7) and at (−7.1, 0, 7.1).

{{< sim file="sims/lighthouse.html" poster="sims/lighthouse.png" title="Lighthouse: light up the ships with a yaw" kind="game" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · Light the ships"}
The beam points along (sin θ, 0, cos θ). sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87.
Choose the yaw for each ship.

::: {.match extra="45°|0°"}
Which yaw lights a ship at (10, 0, 0)?
:   90°

    Why: (sin 90°, 0, cos 90°) = (1, 0, 0).

Which yaw lights a ship at (0, 0, −10)?
:   180°

    Why: (sin 180°, 0, cos 180°) = (0, 0, −1).

Which yaw lights a ship at (5, 0, 8.7)?
:   30°

    Why: (sin 30°, 0, cos 30°) = (0.5, 0, 0.87).

Which yaw lights a ship at (−7.1, 0, 7.1)?
:   −45°

    Why: sin is negative and cos positive: −45°.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7 · A busy night (harder)"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(5, 0, 8.7)|90° only"}
The lamp points at 90°. Which turn reaches a ship at (−10, 0, 0)?
:   180°

    Why: from (1, 0, 0) to (−1, 0, 0) is half a turn.

The beam is 10 long at a yaw of 60°. Where does it end?
:   (8.7, 0, 5)

    Why: 10 × (sin 60°, 0, cos 60°) = 10 × (0.87, 0, 0.5).

The lighthouse stands at (20, 0, 0). Which yaw lights a ship at (30, 0, 0)?
:   90°

    Why: the ship is 10 units in +x from the lighthouse.

Which yaw points the beam straight back, along (0, 0, −1)?
:   180°, the same as −180°

    Why: (sin 180°, 0, cos 180°) = (0, 0, −1).
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- Homogeneous coordinates: (x, y) → (x, y, 1); a 3 × 3 matrix can then move.
- T(tx, ty) has the move in its last column.
- M = T × R × S: scale first, then turn, then move.
- In 3D: (x, y, z, 1) for a point, (x, y, z, 0) for a direction; 4 × 4 matrices.
- Yaw R_y(θ) turns around y: forward (0, 0, 1) → (sin θ, 0, cos θ).
